articles.title: Nobel physics prize awarded for detection of ghostly neutrinos
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 06 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03092-1Francis Halzen wins the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on a pioneering high-energy neutrino observatory at the South Pole.
articles.content:
Credit: Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto via Getty

Belgian physicist Francis Halzen has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work in founding the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and for the discovery of high-energy elusive particles, known as neutrinos, that come from deep in space.

Halzen, who is based at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, will take home all of the 12-million Swedish kronor (US$1.2 million) prize, announced by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm on 6 October.

“It was a great surprise and I obviously didn’t expect it,” said Halzen, speaking to the Nobel committee after the prize was announced. “This reflects on the really courageous people who joined me in this project when really no respectable conservative physicist would have joined me, but many talented people did and that’s why I’m here.”

More than 1 billion neutrinos pass through a hand every second, but high-energy neutrinos are extremely rare and hard to detect. IceCube, based in the South Pole, was designed to study the particles when they fly out of some of the most energetic environments in the Universe, such as supernovae and γ-ray bursts. As neutrinos pass straight through matter, they provide a straight line back to these events, providing researchers with a unique way of probing astrophysical phenomena.

“Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument. His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy,” says Mark Pearce, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics, in a press release announcing the prize.

Looking into the cosmos

Neutrinos are the second most common particle in the Universe, after photons. They are unaffected by magnetic fields and rarely ever interact. In the 1980s, Halzen had the idea to use threads of detectors, lowered more than 1.5 kilometres into holes drilled into the clear ice of the Antarctic, to detect the rare and faint flashes of light when a fast-moving neutrino hits an atom. As long as the volume was big enough, Halzen theorized that the set-up could catch neutrinos and the path would reveal the direction from which they come, allowing researchers to trace their origins in the cosmos.

The resulting detector, the IceCube Neutrino Observatory — an array of 5,160 sensors covering a cubic kilometre — was completed in 2011. “After one and a half decades of development, and another decade of construction, there was no guarantee we would ever see anything,” Halzen told APS news in 2025. “Many people thought we wouldn’t, but we did.”

Within two years, the detector had observed neutrinos from beyond the galaxy and with extreme energies.

“The biggest risk we took is that nobody knew if the kilometer cube detector was actually large enough to detect neutrinos beyond our atmosphere from the Universe and that was our biggest one. But it only took 2 years to detect that,” Halzen told the press conference.

“We found evidence for neutrinos coming from supermassive black holes in other galaxies, and they shine so strongly that when you look at a neutrino sky you don’t see the Milky Way.”

articles.personality_title: Nobel Prize awarded for discovery of high-energy neutrinos from space
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Neutrinos are tiny particles that are very common in the universe but hard to detect because they rarely interact with matter. Scientists have long wanted to study high-energy neutrinos that come from powerful cosmic events like supernovae or black holes.

**What happened** – Francis Halzen, a physicist from the University of Wisconsin–Madison, won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for creating the IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole. This observatory uses over 5,000 sensors buried deep in Antarctic ice to detect rare high-energy neutrinos from space. The project began in the 1980s and finished in 2011. Within two years, it successfully detected neutrinos coming from outside our galaxy.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it provides a new way to study the universe. Neutrinos travel straight from their sources without being affected by magnetic fields, so they help scientists pinpoint where powerful cosmic events happen. This gives researchers a clearer picture of phenomena like supermassive black holes and gamma-ray bursts.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue using IceCube to learn more about the universe’s most energetic events. The observatory’s success may also inspire new detectors and experiments to explore space in ways not possible before.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Francis Halzen’s IceCube Observatory has opened a new path in astronomy by detecting high-energy neutrinos from deep space, earning him the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics.

**Résumé en une phrase** – L’Observatoire IceCube de Francis Halzen a ouvert une nouvelle voie en astronomie en détectant des neutrinos à haute énergie venus de l’espace profond, ce qui lui a valu le prix Nobel de physique 2026.
articles.personality_title_es: Premio Nobel otorgado por el descubrimiento de neutrinos de alta energía del espacio

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos seguirán usando IceCube para aprender más sobre los eventos más energéticos del universo. El éxito del observatorio también podría inspirar nuevos detectores y experimentos para explorar el espacio de formas nuevas.

articles.title: This mysterious hole on the Moon may open into a giant cave
articles.summary: NASA has selected the GIMLI project to investigate whether the Marius Hill Pit opens into a vast underground cave or lava tube. Using radar, seismic sensors, gravity measurements, and cameras, researchers will search beneath the lunar surface and estimate the size of any hidden void. Such caves could preserve clues to the Moon’s volcanic history and potentially provide protected shelters for future astronauts.
articles.content:
NASA has chosen a proposal led by the Planetary Science Institute to determine whether a potentially large cave stretches underground from the opening of a pit on the Moon. If such a cavern exists, it could eventually offer astronauts natural protection from radiation and the dramatic temperature changes experienced on the lunar surface.

The project will receive funding through NASA's Payloads and Research Investigations on the Surface of the Moon (PRISM) program. PRISM sends scientific instruments to the lunar surface aboard spacecraft supplied by providers participating in the Commercial Lunar Payloads Services (CLPS) initiative.

GIMLI Will Probe Beneath the Moon

The selected project, known as the Geophysical Instruments for Marius Lunar pit Investigation, or GIMLI, is led by PSI Associate Director and Senior Scientist Than Putzig. PSI is working with Honeybee Robotics, which will construct much of the mission's equipment and instrumentation. The instruments will travel aboard a lander and rover supplied through the CLPS initiative. PSI's work will also be conducted in partnership with the Norwegian Space Agency.

"GIMLI represents the type of ambitious planetary science that PSI was built to pursue," said PSI Director and CEO Amanda Hendrix. "Than and his team are taking a scientific question we've been studying from orbit and have developed a way to investigate it directly on the Moon. We're excited to have PSI leading this effort and to be partnering with NASA and Honeybee Robotics to learn more about the Moon and its volcanic past."

Scientists studying the Moon from orbit have found compelling evidence that caves and lava tubes could be hidden beneath its surface. GIMLI will concentrate on the Marius Hill Pit (MHP), a large opening located within one of the Moon's most volcanically varied regions. Like other pits identified on the Moon, MHP could provide an entrance into underground structures created by ancient volcanic activity.

Rather than relying only on observations from above, GIMLI will give researchers an opportunity to examine MHP directly from the lunar surface.

Radar and Seismic Sensors Will Search for a Lava Tube

"It's long been a desire of mine to reintroduce intentional active-source seismic methods to planetary science, as it has essentially not been done since the Apollo astronauts conducted the first seismic surveys on the Moon," shared Putzig. "Combining that method with ground-penetrating radar and gravity measurements makes it all the more exciting, as these methods together will allow us to get a much better understanding of subsurface properties -- including the anticipated detection of a lava tube extending away from the Marius Hills pit."

To investigate what lies underground, GIMLI will combine ground penetrating radar, seismic sensors, and a gravimeter. Cameras will also photograph the lunar surface and the exposed walls of the pit. Used together, these instruments will search for a possible underground void extending from MHP and, if one is detected, help scientists estimate its dimensions.

Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin company, will be PSI's commercial partner on the project. The company will provide project management services and construct instrumentation for the active source seismic system, the gravimeter, and the cameras. Honeybee Robotics will also help integrate the scientific instruments onto the lander and rover. Along with PSI, it will lead instrument operations after the spacecraft reaches the lunar surface.

Even No Cave Would Reveal New Lunar Geology

The mission could still produce important discoveries even if researchers find no cave or lava tube. Its measurements could help address another major question: How did the Marius Hill Pit form?

By examining the material surrounding and beneath MHP, scientists could gain new clues about the pit's origin as well as the geology and volcanic history of the wider region.

The team also plans to study more than the possible underground structure. The surrounding area has experienced a long history of volcanic activity, and the walls of MHP expose layers of regolith and lava flows that normally remain buried. Examining these layers could show how lava once moved across and beneath the lunar landscape and whether individual eruptions were separated by long intervals.

Lunar pits are valuable not only because their walls expose otherwise hidden geology. Any underground spaces connected to them could also preserve evidence of the volcanic processes that helped shape the Moon.

A Window Into the Moon's Volcanic Past

"Confirming a substantial lava tube would give us an insight into how volcanism operated on the Moon," explained Gareth Morgan, PSI Senior Scientist and Deputy Principal Investigator on the GIMLI program. "Lava tubes are a common feature of basaltic volcanism on Earth, so identifying them on the Moon means we could use knowledge of such terrestrial caves to better understand lunar history."

In addition to PSI and Honeybee Robotics, the GIMLI team includes Co-Investigators from Boise State University, Johns Hopkins University, the Lunar and Planetary Institute, and the University of Oslo. The Norwegian Space Agency will provide the ground-penetrating radar.

articles.personality_title: NASA’s GIMLI mission will explore a mysterious lunar pit for hidden caves
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – NASA is interested in learning more about the Moon’s underground features, especially caves or lava tubes that formed from ancient volcanic activity. These underground spaces might protect future astronauts from harsh conditions on the Moon’s surface.

**What happened** – NASA chose a project called GIMLI to investigate the Marius Hill Pit, a large hole on the Moon. Led by the Planetary Science Institute (PSI) with help from Honeybee Robotics and the Norwegian Space Agency, the mission will use radar, seismic sensors, gravity measurements, and cameras to look beneath the surface. The instruments will be sent to the Moon on a lander and rover through NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services program.

**Impact** – If GIMLI finds a large cave or lava tube, it could help scientists understand how volcanoes shaped the Moon long ago. Such caves might also serve as natural shelters for astronauts, protecting them from radiation and extreme temperatures. Even if no cave is found, the mission will reveal new information about how the pit formed and the Moon’s volcanic history by studying the layers of rock and soil exposed in the pit’s walls.

**What's next step** – After landing on the Moon, the GIMLI instruments will collect data from the surface and underground. Scientists will analyze this information to map any hidden spaces and learn about the geology of the Marius Hill region. The results could guide future lunar missions and help plan safe places for astronauts to live and work.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s GIMLI mission will explore a lunar pit to discover hidden caves that could reveal the Moon’s volcanic past and offer shelter for future explorers.
articles.personality_title_fr: La mission GIMLI de la NASA va explorer un trou mystérieux sur la Lune à la recherche de grottes cachées
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La NASA souhaite mieux comprendre les caractéristiques souterraines de la Lune, notamment les grottes ou tubes de lave formés par une ancienne activité volcanique. Ces espaces souterrains pourraient protéger les futurs astronautes des conditions difficiles à la surface lunaire.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – La NASA a choisi un projet nommé GIMLI pour étudier le Marius Hill Pit, un grand trou sur la Lune. Dirigée par l’Institute of Planetary Science (PSI) avec l’aide de Honeybee Robotics et de l’Agence spatiale norvégienne, la mission utilisera un radar, des capteurs sismiques, des mesures de gravité et des caméras pour sonder sous la surface. Les instruments seront envoyés sur la Lune à bord d’un atterrisseur et d’un rover grâce au programme Commercial Lunar Payload Services.

**Impact** – Si GIMLI découvre une grande grotte ou un tube de lave, cela aidera les scientifiques à comprendre comment les volcans ont façonné la Lune il y a longtemps. Ces grottes pourraient aussi servir d’abris naturels pour les astronautes, les protégeant des radiations et des températures extrêmes. Même sans grotte, la mission apportera des informations nouvelles sur la formation du trou et l’histoire volcanique de la Lune en étudiant les couches de roche et de sol visibles sur les parois.

**Étape suivante** – Une fois sur la Lune, les instruments de GIMLI recueilleront des données à la surface et sous terre. Les scientifiques analyseront ces informations pour cartographier d’éventuels espaces cachés et mieux connaître la géologie de la région de Marius Hill. Ces résultats pourront guider les futures missions lunaires et aider à planifier des lieux sûrs pour les astronautes.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La mission GIMLI de la NASA explorera un trou lunaire pour découvrir des grottes cachées qui révéleront le passé volcanique de la Lune et offriront un abri aux futurs explorateurs.
articles.personality_title_es: La misión GIMLI de la NASA explorará un agujero lunar misterioso en busca de cuevas ocultas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La NASA quiere entender mejor las características bajo la superficie de la Luna, especialmente cuevas o tubos de lava formados por actividad volcánica antigua. Estos espacios podrían proteger a futuros astronautas de las duras condiciones en la superficie lunar.

**Qué pasó** – La NASA eligió un proyecto llamado GIMLI para estudiar el Marius Hill Pit, un gran agujero en la Luna. Liderado por el Instituto de Ciencias Planetarias (PSI), junto con Honeybee Robotics y la Agencia Espacial Noruega, la misión usará radar, sensores sísmicos, mediciones de gravedad y cámaras para explorar bajo la superficie. Los instrumentos serán enviados en un módulo de aterrizaje y un rover a través del programa Commercial Lunar Payload Services.

**Impacto** – Si GIMLI encuentra una gran cueva o tubo de lava, ayudará a los científicos a entender cómo los volcanes formaron la Luna hace mucho tiempo. Estas cuevas también podrían servir como refugios naturales para los astronautas, protegiéndolos de la radiación y temperaturas extremas. Incluso si no se encuentra cueva, la misión revelará nueva información sobre cómo se formó el agujero y la historia volcánica de la Luna al estudiar las capas de roca y suelo en las paredes.

**Próximo paso** – Después de aterrizar en la Luna, los instrumentos de GIMLI recopilarán datos en la superficie y bajo tierra. Los científicos analizarán esta información para crear mapas de espacios ocultos y conocer mejor la geología de la región de Marius Hill. Los resultados podrán ayudar a planear futuras misiones lunares y lugares seguros para los astronautas.

**Conclusión en una frase** – La misión GIMLI de la NASA explorará un agujero lunar para descubrir cuevas ocultas que revelarán el pasado volcánico de la Luna y ofrecerán refugio a futuros exploradores.
